newsitem.title: Australia: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: NSW AG SAYS EXTRADITION PROCEEDING SMOOTHLY
The New South Wales Attorney General says he's not concerned that extradition documents didn't reach South Africa for the first court appearance yesterday of alleged pedophile Phillip Bell.
This morning Jeff Shaw told ABC radio that the federal government was slow in delivering the document to South African authorities.
Mr Shaw says his office sent the documents to the federal attorney general months ago.
But Mr Shaw says he's been reassurred by the federal government that the Attorney-General's department is going ahead with Mr Bell's extradition without any delay or difficulty.
NATIVE TITLE UNCERTAINTY WILL AFFECT EMPLOYMENT GROWTH
The West Australian Premier says that until the issue of Native title is resolved, there'll be little business investment and no new jobs.
Richard Court says native title uncertainty is a major obstruction to new investment.
He says that in Western Australia investment in many industries, particularly in the resources sector, has stopped because of native title claims.
The WA Premier will meet with New South Wales Premier Bob Carr in Sydney to discuss a uniform response to native title ahead of tomorrow's leaders meeting with the Prime Minister on the issue.
NEW FIRES KEEP VICTORIAN FIREFIGHTERS BUSY
Victorian firefighters have turned their atention to a blaze at Arthur's Seat on the Mornington Peninsula, where it has breached the carpark.
In the Dandenong ranges, homes have been lost at Ferny Creek but blazes at Kalorama and Mount Dandenong have been contained.
Tremont and Basin are the latest trouble spots
MINISTER CALLS FOR HEATWAVE MEASURES AT OPEN
Federal Sports Minister, Warwick Smith has called on the Australian Tennis Open officials to develop measures to cope with heatwave conditions in future touraments.
He's welcomed the decision to close the roof of the main Melbourne Park staduium because of the heat as a victory for commonsense.
Mr Smith says the extreme weather conditions in Melbourne presented a potential danger to the health of players.
He says with the tournament in its second week, all singles matches can be played inside, although he's expressed concern players in doubles matches will still be subjected to the heat.
Mr Smith has urged the organisers to come up with alternative arrangements for future years, to cater for heatwave conditions in the early rounds of the tournament.
SHREDDED WETSUIT COULD BE MISSING WINDSURFER'S
In West Australia, searchers have recovered a shredded wetsuit believed to belong to a German windsurfer missing off the coast of Geraldton.
Search co-ordinator Senior Sergeant Dave Leitch says the wetsuit matches the description given to police by the missing mans friends.
He says the suit was found two-kilometres offshore near Bulla River about 10-kilometres north of Geraldton.
The 41-year-old German tourist was last seen at seven o'clock last night.
An extensive search located the man's board this morning and the wetsuit, harness and glove a short time ago.
Sergeant Leitch says the items are being brought ashore for examination.
COETZER ADVANCES TO SEMIS AT OPEN
South Africa's Amanda Coetzer has advanced to the semi-finals of the women's singles at the Australian Tennis Open.
Coetzer beat American Kimberly Po in two sets, 6-4, 6-1.
She'll meet the winner of tonight's quarter final match between Sabine Appelmans and Mary Pierce.
Earlier, Spain's Carlos Moya became the first player through to the semi-finals of the men's singles.
The 20-year-old defeated fellow countryman, Felix Mantilla, in four sets, in their quarter finals match.
INDONESIAN FISHING BOATS LAND IN DARWIN
The Navy escorted three Indonesian fishing vessels into Darwin harbour this morning.
The vessels have been handed over to the Australian Fisheries Management Authority, which will determine if any Australian fisheries legislation has been breached.
The three boats, with 21 crew on board, were apprehended on Saturday, 4-hundred nautical miles west of Darwin.
NEW STUDY OF ON-LINE ENVIRONMENT
A new study will be launched into the Internet which will include looking at labeling of sexually explicit or violent material.
The study has been commissioned by UNESCO and will be taken on by the Australian Broadcasting Authority.
The ABA's Karen Koomen says it aims to identify the main features of the on-line environment, in relation to content of on-line services.
She says recent technical developments, which enable people to make decisions about what they want to access, will also be looked into.
AUSTRALIA JOINS WTO IN ACTION AGAINST HUNGARY

Australia has joined New Zealand, Argentina, and the United States in taking action against Hungarian farm export subsidies. Hungary is planning to extend existing subsidies from 16 to more than 300 products.
Trade Minister, Tim Fischer, says the action before the World Trade Organisation hasn't been taken lightly, but negotiations with Hungary haven't been successful.
Australia is also seeking to put it's views in action against US import restrictions on prawns from countries which don't require the use of "turtle excluder" devices on warm-water prawn trawlers.
Mr Fischer says Australia supports the US goal of turtle conservation ..but considers the import restrictions unneccessary. - - - -
FUNSHIP HAS FINAL FLING
The P-and-O Fairstar, the longest serving cruise ship in the world, has set sail on its last cruise.
It's headed off for a 10 night South Pacific cruise.
When it returns, the ship, after serving for 23-years, will be replaced by the P-and-O Fair Princess.
Built in 1957, Fairstar served as a troopship before making her migrant voyage to Australia. It began its series of South Pacific and Asian cruises in 1974.
No decision has yet been made as to the Fairstar's future, though negotiations are underway with parties interested in buying the 24-thousand ton vessel.
